title: The Logic of a Prompt & Life

parts.name: Act as
parts.line: A role for the model to take on, which sets its vocabulary, depth and point of view.
parts.logic: Fixes the speaker's standpoint. Like choosing a perspective in an argument, it shapes which premises seem relevant and which words get used. It adds no knowledge or credentials.
parts.pitfall: A role is a costume, not a qualification. A model playing a doctor is not a doctor, so check health, legal or money advice with a real one.
parts.weak: Give me tips for my vegetable garden.
strong: Act as an experienced community gardener.
Give me tips for my vegetable garden.
parts.guess: Which expert voice, level of detail and angle you want.

parts.name: Audience
parts.line: Who will read or use the answer, and what they already know.
parts.logic: Sets the shared background the answer can assume. What counts as informative enough depends on the listener, so the audience fixes how much to explain.
parts.pitfall: A vague audience like 'beginners' helps less than saying what they already know and what they need to do with the answer.
parts.weak: Explain how a mortgage works.
strong: Explain how a mortgage works
to someone buying their first home who has never taken out a loan.
parts.guess: Whether to explain the basics or skip them, and which words the reader knows.

parts.name: Tone
parts.line: The emotional colour of the reply: friendly, formal, firm, playful or calm.
parts.logic: Tone changes how something is said, not what is claimed. Logic separates content from expression, and tone is a request about expression.
parts.pitfall: Tone can blur content. If you ask for 'reassuring', check the reply has not softened a fact you needed to hear plainly.
parts.weak: Write a message telling my team the picnic is cancelled.
strong: Write a
warm, upbeat
message telling my team the picnic is cancelled.
parts.guess: Whether to sound warm, neutral, formal or blunt.

parts.name: Language
parts.line: Which language to answer in, and how plain or technical the wording should be.
parts.logic: A statement only works if both sides read it the same way. Choosing the language and reading level avoids obscurity, which Grice's maxim of Manner warns against.
parts.pitfall: A translation can sound fluent and still be wrong. For anything important, like medicine labels or contracts, ask a fluent speaker to check it.
parts.weak: Write instructions for my neighbour on watering my plants.
strong: Write instructions
in simple Spanish
for my neighbour on watering my plants.
parts.guess: Which language, spelling and reading level to use.

parts.name: Context
parts.line: The background facts of your situation that the answer should build on.
parts.logic: Context supplies the premises: the statements taken as given. A conclusion is only as good as the premises it starts from.
parts.pitfall: False premises give confident nonsense. If your background facts are wrong or out of date, a well-reasoned answer is likely to be wrong too.
parts.weak: Suggest a dinner I can cook tonight.
strong: I have rice, eggs, spinach and twenty minutes, and my partner is vegetarian.
Suggest a dinner I can cook tonight.
parts.guess: Your situation, so it fills the gap with a typical case that may not be yours.

parts.name: Examples
parts.line: One or more samples of what a good answer looks like.
parts.logic: Examples work by induction: from a few cases the model infers a general pattern. Like any induction, the pattern it picks may not be the one you meant.
parts.pitfall: Models can copy examples closely, including their accidents. If all your examples are food words, expect more food words. Vary them on purpose.
parts.weak: Suggest names for my new grey kitten.
strong: Suggest names for my new grey kitten.
Names I like: Pebble, Smudge, Biscuit.
parts.guess: The style, length and pattern you have in your head.

parts.name: Keywords
parts.line: Words or names that must appear, or that pin down the topic.
parts.logic: Keywords mark the subject terms the answer must be about. They work as a relevance test: an answer that never touches them has drifted off the question.
parts.pitfall: A long keyword list turns into word salad. Pick the few terms that truly matter, and check they are used correctly, not just dropped in.
parts.weak: Write a short bio for my bakery's website.
strong: Write a short bio for my bakery's website.
Mention sourdough, our family recipes and the Saturday market.
parts.guess: Which specific names, things or ideas you care about.

parts.name: Terminology
parts.line: Definitions for the words in your request that could mean more than one thing.
parts.logic: Defining terms blocks equivocation, the error of letting one word shift meaning partway through. A definition fixes what a key word refers to from start to finish.
parts.pitfall: Your own words feel obvious to you. Words like 'cheap', 'soon', 'healthy' and 'short' are where misunderstandings hide. Pin them down with numbers.
parts.weak: Give me a training plan for a long-distance race.
strong: Give me a training plan for a long-distance race.
By long-distance I mean a 10 km race, not a marathon.
parts.guess: Which meaning of an ambiguous word you have in mind.

parts.name: Scope
parts.line: What the answer should cover, and what it should leave out.
parts.logic: Scope sets the domain of discourse: the set of things the conversation is about. Claims are judged inside that domain, so a fuzzy domain gives fuzzy answers.
parts.pitfall: A scope that is too narrow can hide what matters. Invite the model to flag anything important just outside your boundary.
parts.weak: Tell me about the history of bicycles.
strong: Tell me about the history of bicycles
from 1860 to 1900, covering design changes only, not racing.
parts.guess: How wide or narrow to go, and what counts as off topic.

parts.name: Limitations
parts.line: Rules the answer must obey, such as length, cost or things to avoid.
parts.logic: Limitations are necessary conditions: an answer that breaks one fails, however good it is otherwise. Meeting every limitation still does not make an answer good enough.
parts.pitfall: Check the answer against each limit yourself. Models sometimes quietly break a rule, such as a word count, while sounding as if they kept it.
parts.weak: Suggest a birthday party activity for ten-year-olds.
strong: Suggest a birthday party activity for ten-year-olds
that works indoors, needs no screens and uses only things most homes already have.
parts.guess: Your hard limits, so it may suggest things you cannot use.

parts.name: Deadline
parts.line: The time frame your task, or the information you need, belongs to.
parts.logic: Mostly practical, not logical. A chat model answers when asked, not on a schedule. The logical part is a time index: many claims are true only as of a date.
parts.pitfall: Models have a knowledge cutoff and may not know today's date. For anything time-sensitive, give the date yourself and check recent facts elsewhere.
parts.weak: Make a study plan for my driving test.
strong: Make a study plan for my driving test,
which is three weeks from today.
parts.guess: Which dates matter, and how current the facts must be.

parts.name: Format
parts.line: The shape of the answer: a list, a table, steps, an email or a short paragraph.
parts.logic: Format is a constraint on form, not content. It answers Grice's advice to be orderly: the same information is easier to check in a shape you can scan.
parts.pitfall: A neat table can make guesses look like facts. Format makes an answer easier to read, not more reliable.
parts.weak: Compare walking, cycling and taking the bus to work.
strong: Compare walking, cycling and taking the bus to work
in a table with one row per option.
parts.guess: Whether you want a list, a table, a paragraph or steps.

parts.name: Objective
parts.line: What you want the answer to achieve: the point of the whole request.
parts.logic: The objective is the conclusion you are reasoning toward. Without it, relevance has no anchor, since Grice tied relevance to the purpose of the conversation.
parts.pitfall: Stating a goal can tilt the answer toward it. Ask 'help me decide' rather than 'convince me', unless you really want only one side.
parts.weak: Tell me about electric cars.
strong: Tell me about electric cars
so I can decide whether my next car should be one.
parts.guess: Why you are asking, so it cannot tell what is useful.

parts.name: Call to action
parts.line: The next step the answer should end on, for you or for the people who read it.
parts.logic: An argument can end in a practical conclusion: a decision about what to do. A call to action turns the reasoning into one clear next step.
parts.pitfall: Pushy calls to action backfire. Ask for one clear, honest next step, not pressure or invented urgency like 'only two places left'.
parts.weak: Write a flyer about our street clean-up.
strong: Write a flyer about our street clean-up
that ends by asking readers to sign up at the library desk.
parts.guess: Whether to end with a next step, and what that step is.

parts.name: Citations
parts.line: Sources the answer should point to, so you can check where each claim comes from.
parts.logic: A citation links a claim to its evidence. It serves Grice's maxim of Quality: do not say things you lack adequate evidence for.
parts.pitfall: Models can invent citations that look real: plausible titles, authors and links that do not exist. Give your own sources when you can, and open every citation before trusting it.
parts.weak: Explain whether reading in dim light harms your eyes.
strong: Using only the health article pasted below,
explain whether reading in dim light harms your eyes,
and say which paragraph supports each point.
parts.guess: Whether you need sources, and which kinds you trust.

parts.name: Statistics
parts.line: Numbers that support a claim, such as counts, averages or rates.
parts.logic: Using a number to support a general claim is a form of induction. A number supports a claim only if it is real, recent and about the right group.
parts.pitfall: Models can produce precise-looking numbers with no real source. Supply your own data where possible, and trace every number to its origin before you repeat it.
parts.weak: Write a paragraph on why our town needs a new crossing.
strong: Write a paragraph on why our town needs a new crossing,
using the traffic survey figures pasted below.
parts.guess: Whether you want numbers, and how precise they must be.

parts.name: Quotes
parts.line: Exact words from a real person or text, repeated word for word.
parts.logic: A quotation is testimony: evidence that someone said something. It counts only if it is accurate and in context. A misquote is a false premise.
parts.pitfall: Models can invent quotations or pin real ones on the wrong person. Paste the exact words yourself, or check any quote against a reliable original.
parts.weak: Write a short speech for my grandmother's 90th birthday.
strong: Write a short speech for my grandmother's 90th birthday,
quoting her favourite saying, which I have written out exactly below.
parts.guess: Whether you want quotes, from whom, and how exact.

parts.name: Points of view
parts.line: Other people's perspectives the answer should consider, not only yours.
parts.logic: Looking from several standpoints tests whether a conclusion holds for everyone affected. A premise that seems obvious from one side may be false or irrelevant from another.
parts.pitfall: Listing views is not the same as weighing them. Two sides shown as equal can hide that one has much better evidence.
parts.weak: Should our family get a dog?
strong: Should our family get a dog?
Consider it from the view of the kids, the parents who will walk it, and our elderly neighbour.
parts.guess: Whose interests and views count, so it may give only one side.

parts.name: Counterarguments
parts.line: The strongest objections to an idea, so you can test it before relying on it.
parts.logic: Popper's idea of falsification: try to refute an idea, not only confirm it. One counterexample can sink a general claim, and objections look for the weak spots.
parts.pitfall: Models tend to agree with the person asking. If you never ask for objections, the lack of any is not evidence your idea is good.
parts.weak: Here is my plan to start selling handmade candles online.
strong: Here is my plan to start selling handmade candles online.
Give me the three strongest reasons it could fail.
parts.guess: Whether you want honest pushback or simple agreement.

parts.name: Analogies
parts.line: A comparison with something familiar that helps explain something new.
parts.logic: An analogy maps the structure of a known case onto a new one. It explains and can suggest, but it never proves; test it by finding where it breaks.
parts.pitfall: Every analogy breaks somewhere. Ask the model to say where its comparison stops working, so you do not carry the wrong part over.
parts.weak: Explain how a computer's memory works.
strong: Explain how a computer's memory works
using an analogy from cooking in a kitchen.
parts.guess: Which familiar things you know well enough to compare against.

parts.name: Questions
parts.line: An invitation for the model to ask you what it needs before it answers.
parts.logic: Questions turn a one-shot guess into a dialogue. Missing premises get supplied instead of assumed, so the answer can be as informative as you need.
parts.pitfall: The model's questions are only as useful as your answers. Answer honestly and specifically; if you guess, it will build on your guess.
parts.weak: Help me write a cover letter for a job.
strong: Help me write a cover letter for a job.
Before you start, ask me up to five questions about the role and my experience.
parts.guess: Everything you forgot to say, silently filled in with typical defaults.
